title: UML for Low-Level Design
description: Visual modeling for LLD interviews: Class diagrams with visibility symbols (+, -, #), relationship notations, Sequence diagrams with lifelines, State machines, and Activity diagrams.

topics.title: UML Class Diagram Notations (+, -, #)
topics.description: Standard UML 3-box compartment notation: Class name, attributes, methods, and visibility specifiers.

sections.title: 1. What is it?
sections.content: A UML Class Diagram is a static structural diagram that describes the structure of a system by showing classes, attributes, operations, and relationships among objects.

sections.title: 2. Why do we need it?
sections.content: In Low-Level Design interviews and technical design documents, UML diagrams communicate architecture instantaneously without getting bogged down in syntax details.

sections.title: 3. Core idea
sections.content: Represent a class as a 3-compartment rectangle: Top = Class Name / Stereotype, Middle = Attributes, Bottom = Methods with visibility modifiers (+ public, - private, # protected, ~ package).

sections.title: 4. How it works
sections.content:
Attribute syntax: [visibility] name : type [= default].
Method syntax: [visibility] name(param: type) : returnType.

sections.title: 8. Real-world example

sections.title: 9. When to use
sections.content: Use class diagrams in Phase 2 of any LLD interview immediately after identifying domain entities.

sections.title: 10. When NOT to use
sections.content: Do not draw private utility helper functions or trivial variables that clutter the diagram during a timed interview.

sections.title: 11. Advantages
sections.content: Universal standard language understood by all software engineers worldwide.

sections.title: 12. Disadvantages
sections.content: Excessive detail can become outdated quickly if not synchronized with code.

sections.title: 13. Variations / Types
sections.content: Conceptual Class Diagrams, Specification Class Diagrams, Implementation Class Diagrams.

sections.title: 14. Common mistakes
sections.content: Writing C++ syntax inside UML boxes (e.g. Writing double balance; instead of the standard UML - balance: double).

sections.title: 15. Interview questions
sections.content: Q: What does an italicized class name or method name signify in UML?

sections.title: 16. Interview answer
sections.content: Answer: An italicized class name indicates an Abstract Class. An italicized method name indicates an Abstract / Pure Virtual Method (e.g. + draw() : void signifies virtual void draw() = 0;).

sections.title: 18. Summary
sections.content: UML class diagrams are the standard visual shorthand for expressing object-oriented architecture in Low-Level Design.

topics.title: UML Relationship Arrows & Multiplicities
topics.description: Mastering UML connector symbols: Inheritance, Realization, Composition, Aggregation, Association, and Dependency.

sections.title: 1. What is it?
sections.content: UML Relationships define the structural and behavioral links between classes: Inheritance (──▷), Realization (..▷), Composition (──◆), Aggregation (──◇), Association (──>), and Dependency (..>).

sections.title: 2. Why do we need it?
sections.content: Accurately communicating ownership, lifecycle binding, and coupling is essential in design discussions.

sections.title: 3. Core idea
sections.content: Solid line with filled diamond = strong lifetime ownership (Composition). Solid line with hollow diamond = shared container (Aggregation). Dashed line with open arrow = temporary use (Dependency).

sections.title: 4. How it works
sections.content: Multiplicities denote quantities (e.g. 1, 0..1, *, 1..*). In C++, 1..* maps to a container member like std::vector<T>.

sections.title: 7. Code walkthrough
sections.content:
Line 27 (Composition): Engine engine; is directly embedded.
Line 28 (Aggregation): Driver* currentDriver; does not own Driver memory.
Line 35 (Dependency): navigateTo(const GpsCoordinate& target) receives GPS as a temporary parameter without storing it.

sections.title: 8. Real-world example
sections.content: Enterprise software architecture blueprints (e.g. AWS / Google Cloud reference architectures).

sections.title: 9. When to use
sections.content: Use precise relationship arrows on system architecture whiteboards to clarify object lifecycles.

sections.title: 10. When NOT to use
sections.content: Do not draw Dependency arrows for every standard library type (like std::string) to prevent diagram clutter.

sections.title: 11. Advantages
sections.content: Unambiguous specification of lifetime, ownership, and coupling.

sections.title: 12. Disadvantages
sections.content: Distinguishing Aggregation vs Association can be subjective in informal discussions.

sections.title: 13. Variations / Types
sections.content: Bidirectional Association, Unidirectional Association, Multiplicity bounds (1..*).

sections.title: 14. Common mistakes
sections.content: Confusing Composition (filled diamond) with Aggregation (hollow diamond).

sections.title: 15. Interview questions
sections.content: Q: What is the difference between an Association and a Dependency in C++ code?

sections.title: 16. Interview answer
sections.content: Answer: An Association is a structural link where class A holds a persistent reference or pointer to class B as a member variable. A Dependency is a transient behavioral relationship where class A uses class B only as a method parameter or local variable inside a function body.

expectedEntities.name: Hospital

sections.title: 18. Summary
sections.content: Mastering UML relationship symbols allows you to express object lifecycles and coupling with precision in system design interviews.

topics.title: Sequence Diagrams & Lifelines
topics.description: Visualizing dynamic runtime message passing, synchronous calls, return messages, and object lifelines over time.

sections.title: 1. What is it?
sections.content: A UML Sequence Diagram is an interaction diagram that shows how objects collaborate over time by depicting message exchanges along vertical lifelines.

sections.title: 2. Why do we need it?
sections.content: Class diagrams show static structure, but Sequence diagrams show dynamic runtime behavior (e.g. what happens when a user clicks 'Buy Now').

sections.title: 3. Core idea
sections.content: Time flows downward. Vertical dashed lines represent object lifelines. Horizontal solid arrows represent synchronous method calls; dashed arrows represent return values.

sections.title: 4. How it works
sections.content: Components: Lifelines (Client, OrderService, PaymentGateway), Activation Bars (execution period), Synchronous Messages (──>), Asynchronous Messages (──>>), and Self-Calls.

sections.title: 5. Visual explanation
sections.content: Order Checkout Sequence Flow:

callout.title: Sequence Flow: Checkout Order
callout.text:
1. Customer -> checkout(cartId) -> OrderService
2. OrderService -> calculateTotal(cartId) -> CartService
3. OrderService -> charge(amount) -> PaymentGateway
4. PaymentGateway --> [TX_SUCCESS] --> OrderService
5. OrderService -> sendReceipt(email) -> NotificationService
6. OrderService --> [OrderConfirmed] --> Customer

sections.title: 8. Real-world example
sections.content: OAuth2 3-way authorization flows, payment processing gateways, and database 2-phase commit protocols.

sections.title: 9. When to use
sections.content: Use sequence diagrams whenever explaining complex multi-object business workflows in an interview.

sections.title: 10. When NOT to use
sections.content: Do not draw sequence diagrams for trivial single-class CRUD operations.

sections.title: 11. Advantages
sections.content: Visually highlights bottlenecks, redundant round-trips, and order of execution.

sections.title: 12. Disadvantages
sections.content: Can become wide and difficult to read if more than 6 lifelines are involved.

sections.title: 13. Variations / Types
sections.content: Synchronous Sequence, Asynchronous Sequence with reply loops, Communication Diagrams.

sections.title: 14. Common mistakes
sections.content: Omitting return arrows or mixing up asynchronous message notation.

sections.title: 15. Interview questions
sections.content: Q: What is an activation box in a UML sequence diagram?

sections.title: 16. Interview answer
sections.content: Answer: An Activation Box (or execution occurrence) is a thin vertical rectangle placed on an object's lifeline representing the exact time period during which that object is actively executing a method on the CPU or call stack.

sections.title: 18. Summary
sections.content: Sequence diagrams provide a crystal-clear timeline of runtime interactions across collaborating system objects.

topics.title: State Machines & Activity Diagrams
topics.description: Modeling object lifecycle state transitions, guard conditions, and algorithmic flowcharts in UML.

sections.title: 1. What is it?
sections.content: A UML State Machine Diagram models the lifecycle states of a single entity (e.g. Order: CREATED -> PAID -> SHIPPED). A UML Activity Diagram models business workflow algorithms and decision branches.

sections.title: 2. Why do we need it?
sections.content: Complex real-world entities (Vending Machines, Orders, Hotel Bookings) have strict state-dependent behaviors. State diagrams visualize valid and invalid transitions.

sections.title: 3. Core idea
sections.content: States are rounded rectangles. Transitions are arrows labeled with Event [Guard] / Action.

sections.title: 4. How it works
sections.content: In C++, finite state machines are implemented using the State Design Pattern or an enum class State with guarded transition methods.

sections.title: 8. Real-world example
sections.content: TCP connection lifecycle (LISTEN -> SYN_SENT -> ESTABLISHED -> FIN_WAIT -> CLOSED).

sections.title: 9. When to use
sections.content: Use state diagrams when an entity's behavior changes fundamentally based on internal state.

sections.title: 10. When NOT to use
sections.content: Do not create state diagrams for stateless calculation utilities.

sections.title: 11. Advantages
sections.content: Prevents illegal state transitions and unhandled edge-case bugs.

sections.title: 12. Disadvantages
sections.content: State transition tables can grow to $O(N^2)$ if there are many states.

sections.title: 13. Variations / Types
sections.content: Hierarchical State Machines (Statecharts), Activity Flowcharts.

sections.title: 14. Common mistakes
sections.content: Allowing transitions from terminal states (e.g. mutating an order after it has been CANCELLED).

sections.title: 15. Interview questions
sections.content: Q: What design pattern is best suited for complex state machines with dozens of transitions?

sections.title: 16. Interview answer
sections.content: Answer: The State Design Pattern, where each state is encapsulated as its own polymorphic class (e.g. HasMoneyState, DispensingState) implementing a common IVendingState interface, eliminating massive switch-case blocks.

sections.title: 17. Practice problem
sections.content: Implement an AudioPlayer FSM supporting PLAYING, PAUSED, and STOPPED states.

practice.title: Audio Player FSM
practice.problemStatement: Implement AudioPlayer state transitions for play, pause, and stop.

sections.title: 18. Summary
sections.content: State machine and activity diagrams model the dynamic lifecycle and algorithmic workflows of mission-critical systems.
